narrative:
The model estimated a 62.9% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, it placed your application closer to the failure group than the passing group, so the law school denied admission to reduce that risk.

The strongest factor in this decision was your undergraduate GPA. Your 3.70 is above the accepted-student average of 3.23, and this factor pushed the prediction toward passing. However, it was outweighed by your class standing in law school. Your third-year decile was the second most influential factor and pushed strongly toward failure: you were in the first decile (1.00) while accepted students averaged around 5.79. Your first-year decile was the third most influential factor and also pushed toward failure: you were again at 1.00, compared with an accepted average of about 6.00. Thus, despite a strong GPA, consistently very low class rank in both early and later law-school years was the clearest warning sign. Your LSAT score of 22, well below the accepted average of 37.18, adds further concern even though it was not among the top three drivers.

Next, ask admissions for feedback, meet with academic advising, and build a concrete plan to address the low class standing. Consider retaking the LSAT if feasible, seeking structured bar-exam readiness support, and applying when you can show improved academic performance or a stronger test record.
